title: How to Centralize Payments Across Booking Channels for Hotel Groups in Southeast Asia
summary: See how hotel groups in Southeast Asia can centralize payments across booking channels, cut reconciliation work, and scale to new properties with Xendit. The post How to Centralize Payments Across Booking Channels for Hotel Groups in Southeast Asia appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
Southeast Asia's


[online accommodation market](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/asean-online-accommodation-market) reached


**USD 27.67 billion in 2025** and is on track to hit


**USD 46.48 billion by 2031** , growing at


**9.03% a year** .


As more of that demand moves online,


**hotel groups** are processing


**higher transaction volumes** across direct booking websites, online travel agents (OTAs), travel agents, and on-property channels. The pressure to


**centralize payments** **across booking channels** grows with every new property and every new market you add.


A single hotel can manage those channels with a simple payment setup. For a group running multiple properties, that same growth tends to scatter payment operations across more channels, systems, and records.


Each channel, payment method, and property-level system can produce its own transaction records, which makes portfolio-wide visibility and reconciliation harder just as the group is growing fastest.


A


**centralized hotel payment** setup brings collection, reporting, and reconciliation for every property and booking channel into one connected system, instead of a separate process for each. Setting this up keeps your finance operations manageable as the portfolio grows, because otherwise every new property adds another set of records to chase.


**Here is what this guide covers:**


- Why hotel payment operations fragment as a group adds properties, channels, and markets


- What that fragmentation costs across visibility, reconciliation, and guest experience


- What a centralized hospitality payment setup should provide


- How Xendit supports centralized hotel payments across Southeast Asia


- How a centralized setup supports adding properties and entering new markets


## **Why hotel payment operations fragment as your group grows**


**Payment fragmentation** is rarely the result of one decision. It builds up as a hotel group


**grows through different channels and systems** , each added to solve an immediate need at the time.


That build-up is more pronounced in Southeast Asia as one stay can be booked through an OTA such as Agoda or Traveloka, a direct website, a travel agent, or the front desk, and each channel settles through its own mechanism. For example, an OTA booking might reach you as a virtual credit card (VCC) that finance charges and reconciles by hand, a direct booking clears through the hotel's own gateway, and a walk-in is recorded at the property.


Payments in hospitality have also modernized more slowly than in sectors such as e-commerce and retail, so many hotels still run on legacy systems that were never built to bring these flows together. Each property in a group can carry its own version of this setup, so the


**disconnected records** multiply with every location and market you add.


Knowing where that fragmentation starts makes it easier to see what a centralized setup has to fix, so it helps to look at the


**three patterns behind fragmented hotel payment** operations:


- **Multiple booking channels create separate payment flows** A guest can book through your direct website, an OTA, a travel agent, or at the front desk, and each route can follow its own payment, verification, and reporting process.


According to one


[ASEAN online accommodation market analysis](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/asean-online-accommodation-market) , third-party portals accounted for 69.02% of online accommodation bookings in 2025, while direct and captive portals are the fastest-growing channel at a 15.51% CAGR through 2031.


For your business, the two largest sources of bookings are both expanding, so the number of separate payment flows you manage keeps growing.


-


### **Properties may run on different systems** Each hotel or market can use its own payment providers, bank accounts, dashboards, and reconciliation workflows, often inherited from before the group acquired or onboarded the property.


The more properties you add, the harder portfolio-wide reporting becomes, because head office is reading from systems that were never designed to line up.


-


### **Guest payment preferences vary by market and booking value** International and high-value bookings lean more on card payments, while domestic guests within Southeast Asia often prefer local options such as QR payments, bank transfers, and e-wallets, including QRIS in Indonesia, GCash in the Philippines, PromptPay in Thailand, and FPX in Malaysia.


For a group operating in more than one country, each property may need a different payment mix, and supporting all of them through separate integrations multiplies the operational load.


###

Left unmanaged, these three patterns do more than complicate operations, because they carry a measurable cost across visibility, staff time, and the guest experience. Each of those costs lands in a different part of the operation.


## **What fragmented payments cost multi-property hotel groups**


When payments are scattered across channels and systems, the cost compounds as transaction volume grows and falls into


**four connected areas** :


- **Limited portfolio-wide visibility** Head office can struggle to see transaction status, settlement activity, and cash flow across every property from one place.


[Sahid Hotels & Resorts](https://www.xendit.co/en-id/case-study/sahid-hotels-resorts/) , which runs 26 properties across 21 cities in Indonesia, previously had its finance team review and prepare reports separately for each property. After centralizing with Xendit, transaction data across all properties can be


**managed** from


**a single dashboard.** For your business, that


**consolidation** is what lets head office act on current numbers instead of waiting for each property to report in.


- **Manual booking and payment matching** Finance and reservation teams often match transaction records to booking references by hand, especially for deposits and bank transfers.


At


[RedDoorz](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/reddoorz-boosts-efficiency-in-finance-operations-with-various-xendit-solutions/) , which lists more than 3,600 properties across Southeast Asia,


**virtual credit card (VCC) transactions** once required manual entry and reconciliation that took up to five minutes each before the process was


**automated** through Xendit.


With hundreds of bookings coming in each day, this manual matching adds up quickly and pulls staff away from more useful work.


- **Slower reconciliation across properties** Every transaction has to be matched to the correct property, booking channel, reservation, amount, and settlement record.


**Centralizing** this data with Xendit


**reduced the manpower** Sahid needed for


[reconciliation by 22%](https://www.xendit.co/en-id/case-study/sahid-hotels-resorts/) , while removing the need to cross-check records across its 26 properties.


For a growing group, that saved time means your finance team can take on more properties without the group hiring more people each time it grows.


- **Inconsistent guest payment experiences** Available methods, confirmation times, and payment instructions can differ between properties and channels, which guests notice.


When RedDoorz


**tokenized** e-wallet payments to remove repeated OTP and PIN steps for returning customers, it recorded a


[34% uplift](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/reddoorz-boosts-efficiency-in-finance-operations-with-various-xendit-solutions/) in e-wallet


**conversion** compared with non-tokenized transactions.


The lesson for your business is that a consistent, low-friction payment experience protects completed bookings, along with guest satisfaction. Seeing the cost in these terms points to what a centralized payment setup actually needs to deliver.

## **What a centralized hospitality payment setup should provide**


A centralized setup should


**solve the fragmentation problem** at its root, giving head office one view of the portfolio while each property keeps the control it needs day to day.


A few core


**capabilities** make the difference for a multi-property group:


- **Centralized visibility across properties** Head office needs to see payment activity across the full portfolio, while each property can still view and report on its own transactions. This gives your regional finance team the group-level picture they need for oversight and cash flow, without losing the property-level detail for questions about any single hotel.


- **Flexible account structures** Transactions should be organized by property, brand, market, or business unit, so your reports and daily controls follow the same structure as the business. As you add properties or enter new markets, this structure keeps reporting clean instead of forcing everything through one undifferentiated account.


- **Local payment methods through one integration** A hotel group should be able to support the relevant methods in each market without building and maintaining a separate integration per property or country. This keeps the


**payment method mix** local where it needs to be while the work of managing those methods stays in one place.


- **Real-time payment status** Reservation and front-office teams need clear confirmation of whether a payment has succeeded, is still pending, or has failed. Accurate


**real-time status** is what prevents rooms from being held on unconfirmed payments or released on ones that actually cleared.


- **Consistent reconciliation data** **Payment and settlement information** should follow the same structure across every property and channel. When the data lines up, reconciliation becomes a check instead of a rebuild, which is the difference that scales as volume grows.


When your hotel group has centralized visibility, flexible account structures, local payment methods through one integration, real-time payment status, and consistent reconciliation data, you can run payments across the whole portfolio without the fragmentation building up as you grow. Getting there depends on the right payment infrastructure.

## **FAQ: Centralizing payments for multi-property hotel groups in Southeast Asia**


### **How can a multi-property hotel group manage payments from all its properties in one place?**


You can use


**Xendit's**[XenPlatform](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/xenplatform/) to create sub-accounts for each property or business unit, giving head office one view of payment activity across the portfolio while each property keeps its transactions and fund flows organized. This replaces property-by-property checking with a single dashboard and reporting structure. It is the same approach Xendit uses to support large hotel networks across Southeast Asia.


### **How do you reconcile hotel payments across different booking channels?**


Reconciliation gets easier when payment and settlement data follows one consistent structure across every property and channel, so each transaction can be matched to the right property, reservation, amount, and settlement record. With


**Xendit** , hotel groups manage this from a


[centralized dashboard](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/xenplatform-overview) with


[API integration](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/payments-via-api-overview) , which removes the need to cross-check records property by property. Finance teams can then focus on exceptions instead of rebuilding reports from scattered sources.


### **Can one Xendit integration cover all the payment methods guests use across Southeast Asia?**


Yes. Through a single


[Xendit integration](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-products) , hotels can accept cards, virtual accounts, bank transfers, e-wallets, and QR payments, including


[local methods](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) such as QRIS in Indonesia, GCash in the Philippines, PromptPay in Thailand, and FPX in Malaysia. This lets each property offer a locally relevant payment method mix without your team building and maintaining a separate integration for every market.


### **What happens to a guest's booking if a payment fails or is delayed?**


Reservation and front-office teams need to know immediately whether a payment has succeeded, is pending, or has failed, so rooms are not held on unconfirmed payments or released on ones that cleared.


**Xendit** provides real-time


[payment status](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transaction-status) and maintains high processing reliability, so confirmations stay dependable even during peak booking periods when volumes rise. This protects both the guest experience and confirmed revenue.


### **Does centralizing payments make it easier to add new properties or enter new markets?**


It does. When payment operations run through one centralized setup, adding a property or a market becomes a configuration step instead of a new integration project, because visibility, reporting, and guest payment options stay consistent across the portfolio.
